description: Evaluation queries for the Homework #2 retrieval layer. `category` records why each query is in the set; `expected_documents` is the document_id(s) a good retriever should surface, used for a mechanical hit/miss verdict. `comment` is authored by hand AFTER inspecting a real run — it is the graded relevance judgement and must never be a placeholder. Homework #3 adds `hw3_comment` (the per-query baseline-vs-improved judgement rendered into outputs/retrieval_comparison.md) and the top-level `hw3_conclusion` — both follow the same authored-after-a-real-run rule. Homework #4 adds `hw4_comment` (the per-question grounded-answer judgement rendered into outputs/rag_answers_examples.md), the top-level `hw4_conclusion`, and `hw4_prompt_improvements` (the per-case before/after write-up rendered into outputs/prompt_improvements.md) — all three follow the same authored-after-a-real-run rule.
hw3_conclusion: Metadata filtering delivered the reliability gain and hybrid search delivered the precision gain; the combination is strictly better than either alone. Filter-only lifted top-3 expected-document precision from 0.889 to 0.926 by evicting foreign-document chunks (q09's CQRS leak disappears) while never changing a correct result — the conservative zero-or-tie → unfiltered rule means it cannot misfire on ambiguous queries. Hybrid-only produced the single largest per-query win — q05, where inference stays unfiltered and BM25's lexical match on the ledger/immutable-events vocabulary promoted two genuinely better chunks — but on its own it also REGRESSED q09 (a foreign CQRS chunk reached top-1 on the word 'event') and leaked a migration chunk into q06's top-3, dropping the top-1 hit rate to 0.89. Combined, the filter constrains exactly that leakage while hybrid re-ranks within the filtered set: top-3 precision 0.963 with the top-1 hit rate back at 1.00. So the biggest effect comes from metadata filtering — it both adds precision and removes hybrid's failure mode — while the biggest single-query improvement comes from BM25 on the one query filtering cannot touch. Two honest caveats: with four document types mapping 1:1 to four documents, a correct filter is equivalent to selecting the right document, so its measured effect is an upper bound a larger corpus would not reproduce as strongly; and q08 shows the breadcrumb title-token boost reordering hits within the right document to a slightly worse top-1 — hybrid is a net win in aggregate, not uniformly per query.
hw4_conclusion:
Grounded QA works on this corpus, and the two fallback gates carry different weight than expected. Across the ten questions the v3 prompt answered nine and refused one, every answer carried at least one citation (9/9), no answer cited a chunk that was not supplied (0 fabricated), and no answer was produced from an empty context. The refusal is the result worth trusting least on its own, so it was measured against its counterfactual rather than asserted: case-1 runs q10 through the assignment's own starting prompt over the identical retrieved chunks and gets a confident eight-step tutorial on LoRA, Hugging Face and gradient clipping — not one word of which comes from a logistics corpus. The same question under v2 returns the refusal sentence. That single pair is the homework's core evidence: the retrieval was identical, so the hallucination was entirely the prompt's doing. 

The two gates did not contribute equally. The relevance floor fired exactly once (q10, top 0.266 against a 0.35 threshold) and the prompt rule never had to override a context it did receive — no in-corpus question was refused. But the floor is thinner than the aggregate suggests, and the per-question data says so: q05 cleared it at 0.412 on a foreign-document chunk the answer then did not cite, while the two chunks that actually answered scored 0.354 and 0.361 — 0.004 and 0.011 above the line. q04, the vocabulary-mismatch paraphrase HW2 flagged, cleared at 0.413. Two of the nine answered questions sit within 0.07 of refusal (q05 at +0.062 and q04 at +0.063) and a third, q06, within 0.09 (+0.081). The floor earned its place on the one query it was built for, and it is one recalibration away from costing a correct answer. 

What generation adds over retrieval is clearest where HW2's own complaints were sharpest. HW2 judged q09 unresolved because "the POD-to-settlement link is retrievable but not cleanly isolated in one chunk"; the model assembled it from three and cited all three. HW2 called q01's top-1 imprecise because an overlap tail pushed the definition to top-3; generation reads all of top-k, so the chunk boundary stopped mattering. And HW2/HW3's 0.582-vs-0.581 tie on q02 — which HW3 spent BM25 on breaking — turned out to be irrelevant once both chunks were in context. Several defects that were genuinely worth fixing at the retrieval grade simply stop being defects once a model reads the whole top-k. The inherited limits that do survive are the ones about content rather than ordering: q08's breadcrumb-inflated score still decides which chunks arrive, and no prompt rule can repair a chunk that was never retrieved.

hw4_prompt_improvements.case-1: **The load-bearing result.** Under v1 — the assignment's own starting prompt — the model answered a question its context could not support, at length and with total confidence: an eight-step tutorial covering dataset preparation, Hugging Face Transformers, tokenization, hyperparameters, LoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Every word of it came from the model's general knowledge; the three retrieved chunks were about monolith migration and CQRS. Under v2, over the identical chunks, the answer is the refusal sentence and nothing else. What v2 adds is a role, the only-from-context rule, and a verbatim refusal sentence, and this case cannot distinguish which of the three did the work — but it settles the question the 5-point fallback row actually asks. Retrieval was held constant, so the hallucination was the prompt's doing and the refusal is the prompt's fix. It also shows why the relevance floor alone would have been insufficient evidence: the floor decides what the model sees, and only the prompt decides what the model does about seeing nothing.
hw4_prompt_improvements.case-2: **Citations are not free — they have to be demanded.** v2 already answers q01 correctly and stays inside the context; its grounding is not in question. What it does not do is say where the answer came from: zero citations, and a reader has no way to check it short of re-running retrieval. v3 adds the mandatory inline [chunk_id] rule and the same question comes back citing two chunks, both of which were genuinely in the context. The answer also grew a third sentence — the backhaul-optimization point from chunk_011 — which suggests the citation rule pushed the model to use more of the context rather than settle for the first chunk that sufficed. This is the isolated evidence for the 10-point citation row: same question, same chunks, one rule added, 0 → 2 citations.
hw4_prompt_improvements.case-3: **The honest one — the cumulative jump did NOT prevent a hallucination here.** v1 was expected to drift on q05, whose context genuinely spans two documents and whose subject (event sourcing) is exactly the kind of thing a model knows independently. It did not drift: v1's answer is substantively grounded, and its specifics — posting a load, repricing, tendering, booking, delivery — track the corpus rather than invented detail. The real v1→v3 differences are attribution and discipline: v1 cites nothing, so a reader cannot verify a correct answer; v3 cites cqrs_chunk_008 and honours the five-sentence bound. Both versions correctly ignored the foreign migration chunk sitting in the same context. The finding is that a naive prompt is not reliably wrong — it is unreliably right, which is worse, because it means case-1's hallucination could not have been predicted from a single well-behaved sample. That is the argument for keeping all three prompts runnable rather than documenting them as prose.

queries.query: What is a backhaul and why does it matter to a carrier?
queries.comment: Relevant. All three hits are from the right document and the Key Domain Vocabulary section does define backhaul. But top-1 opens mid-sentence ("time and handling risk...") because it carries an overlap tail, so the definition a reader wants is actually in top-3. Right section, imprecise chunk.
queries.hw3_comment: No change at top-1 — the direct query was already resolved correctly, and the filter (concept-guide, correctly inferred) had nothing to evict from an all-primer top-3. Hybrid only reshuffled rank 3 within the same document. The improved pipeline's job here was to not break an easy case, and it didn't.
queries.hw4_comment: Grounded and cited. The answer fuses chunk_018's definition with chunk_011's backhaul-optimization point and cites both. Worth noting against the Homework #2 comment on this same query: HW2's complaint was that top-1 opens mid-sentence ("time and handling risk...") so the definition a reader wants sits at top-3. The generation layer makes that complaint moot — it reads all of top-k, so an imprecise chunk boundary costs nothing once a model is assembling the answer.

queries.query: How does CQRS separate the write model from the read models?
queries.comment: Relevant. Top-1 and top-2 tie at 0.582 and both come from Why CQRS Fits Freight; top-2 is the better answer because it opens with the definition, so the ordering between two near-identical scores is effectively arbitrary. Top-3 is a reasonable continuation.
queries.hw3_comment: Top-1 and top-2 unchanged (filter correctly inferred architecture-guide; all hits were already CQRS chunks). BM25 agreed with the semantic top-1 (#1 in both rankings), which resolves HW2's observation that the 0.582 tie made the order arbitrary — the lexical branch now breaks that tie deliberately rather than by chance. Rank 3 swapped to the Operational Realities chunk on keyword strength; lateral, same document.
queries.hw4_comment: Grounded and cited, drawing on both chunk_001 and chunk_002. This retires the tie HW2 and HW3 both flagged: the two chunks scored 0.582/0.581 and HW2 judged the ordering between them "effectively arbitrary", while HW3 noted BM25 broke the tie deliberately rather than by chance. For answer generation the tie never mattered — both chunks are in context and the answer uses both. Top-1 ordering is a retrieval-grade concern that generation is largely indifferent to.

queries.query: What is the strangler-fig pattern for migrating a monolith?
queries.comment: Highly relevant — the best result in the set. Top-1 (0.685) opens with the definition itself and all three hits are the Strangler-Fig Execution section in reading order. A direct query whose vocabulary matches the corpus is the easy case, and it behaves like one.
queries.hw3_comment: Unchanged at top-1 and top-2 — the strongest baseline result stays the strongest improved result (semantic #1 = BM25 #1). Rank 3 swapped to the document's introduction chunk via BM25's liking for title tokens; marginally less useful than the baseline's in-order continuation, but the same document and a reasonable entry point.
queries.hw4_comment: The cleanest result in the set, as it was for HW2 and HW3. Highest retrieval score (0.685), and the answer covers the pattern, its incremental-reversibility rationale, the facade step, and the lift-the-data warning — cited to the two chunks that carry them. Nothing to fault.

queries.query: How do I stop my trucks from driving back empty after a delivery?
queries.comment: Partially relevant. The paraphrase deliberately avoids the word 'backhaul' and the retriever still finds the right document, but no retrieved chunk leads with the backhaul definition, and the score falls to 0.413 from 0.536 for the same concept asked directly (q01). This is the vocabulary-mismatch penalty made visible.
queries.hw3_comment: Top-1 unchanged. The filter (concept-guide, inferred from 'trucks'/'delivery') was already satisfied, and hybrid reshuffled ranks 2–3 within the right document. The HW2 finding stands mostly unrepaired: when a paraphrase avoids the corpus vocabulary, BM25 has as little to grip as the embedding does — hybrid search helps lexical matches, and this query deliberately offers none.
queries.hw4_comment: Grounded and cited, and the most interesting near-miss in the set. Top semantic is 0.413 — only 0.063 above the 0.35 floor, and the lowest of any answered question. HW2 measured this exact query at 0.413 and called it "the vocabulary-mismatch penalty made visible"; that penalty now sits directly against the fallback threshold. The answer is correct (it names backhaul from chunk_018, the very chunk HW2 said did not lead with the definition), but this is the query that would break first if the floor were raised.

queries.query: Why would you keep every change as a permanent record instead of just updating a row in a table?
queries.comment: Partially relevant. Top-1 is the correct document and genuinely about immutable events, but top-2 and top-3 leak into the migration and scaling documents — the paraphrase 'permanent record instead of updating a row' matches generic write-path language across the whole corpus. The only query whose top-3 spans three documents.
queries.hw3_comment: The flagship hybrid win, on exactly the query the filter cannot help (inference correctly returns none — the vocabulary is ambiguous). BM25 promoted Event Sourcing Basics ('never deleted. A correction is expressed as a further event, in the way a ledger is corrected by a reversing entry') and Projections And Read Models from semantic ranks 4–5 into the top-2 — both better answers than the baseline's top-1. The three-document leak shrinks to one foreign chunk at rank 3; top-3 precision goes from 1/3 to 2/3.
queries.hw4_comment: Grounded and cited, but the retrieval scores tell the more important story. The floor was cleared at 0.412 by monolith_to_microservices_migration_chunk_017 — a foreign-document chunk the answer then did not cite. The two chunks that actually answer the question score 0.354 and 0.361, barely 0.004 and 0.011 above the floor. So the gate was opened by a chunk that contributed nothing, and the useful evidence only just qualified. The model's own selection was correct — it cited cqrs_chunk_008 and ignored the migration chunk sitting in the same context — which is grounding working exactly as intended on a mixed context.

queries.query: How can I release new code without users noticing any interruption?
queries.comment: Relevant. Despite the lowest-band score (0.431), all three hits are the Zero-Downtime Deployments section and top-1 opens on exactly the right sentence. Score magnitude and usefulness are not the same thing — a low absolute score with tight section clustering is a good result.
queries.hw3_comment: The two Zero-Downtime Deployments chunks swapped places (BM25 prefers the additive-API-changes chunk; the semantic branch still ranks the rollout-mechanism chunk first) — a lateral move within the right section. The filter earned its keep at rank 3: hybrid-only leaked a migration chunk into the top-3 on shared deployment vocabulary, and the playbook filter kept the result all-playbook. Without the filter this query would have LOST precision to hybrid.
queries.hw4_comment: Grounded and cited (chunks 010 and 011), and it exposes a real property of the floor: the retrieved set includes scaling_chunk_004 at 0.266 — the same value, to displayed precision, as q10's top score, the one that triggers a full refusal (0.26584 against 0.26609; they round alike rather than being equal). The floor is evaluated on the best score in the set, not per chunk, so a sub-threshold chunk rides along into the context whenever a stronger sibling clears the gate. Here it did no harm (the model cited neither) but the mechanism is worth stating plainly.

queries.query: How is data kept consistent between the old system and the new services during a migration?
queries.comment: Highly relevant. All three hits are the Keeping Data In Sync Mid-Migration section, covering dual-write, read switch, and duplicate handling. The question spans two documents conceptually, but the migration document answers it completely, so a single-document result is correct rather than narrow.
queries.hw3_comment: Top-1 moved to the chunk that opens on the dual-write premise ('both the monolith and a new service hold data for the same context, and both must be correct') — a better lead than the baseline's mid-section chunk. The case-study filter formally excludes the second expected document (CQRS), but the baseline never surfaced it either and HW2 already judged the migration document a complete answer; the conservative-inference risk this query was designed to expose did not materialize as a loss.
queries.hw4_comment: Grounded and cited to both chunks, and this is where generation adds something retrieval could not. The answer separates two distinct mechanisms — event-driven synchronization over a durable log, and record-level parity verification gating the read switch — and attributes each to its own chunk. HW3 noted the case-study filter formally excludes the second expected document (CQRS); that exclusion still costs nothing, because the migration document answers the question completely.

queries.query: What has to be true for the platform to handle 5,000 requests per second?
queries.comment: Relevant, but partly for the wrong reason. Top-1 directly addresses what the 5,000 requests per second figure does and does not tell you. The score (0.646) is inflated by lexical overlap: the exact phrase appears in the document title, which the breadcrumb prepends to every chunk of that document. Semantically right, but this query cannot distinguish semantic from keyword matching.
queries.hw3_comment: The honest negative example. BM25 promoted the Observability chunk to top-1 over the Load Profile chunk that HW2 judged the best answer — the breadcrumb repeats '5,000 Requests per Second' in every chunk of this document, so the lexical branch amplifies exactly the title-token inflation HW2 flagged on the semantic side. Still the right document, still a hit, and the displaced chunk sits at rank 2, but qualitatively the top-1 got slightly worse. This is the design doc's breadcrumb-bias limitation showing up on schedule.
queries.hw4_comment: Grounded and cited to three chunks. The honest caveat HW2 and HW3 both recorded still applies underneath: the 0.646 top score is inflated by the breadcrumb repeating "5,000 Requests per Second" from the document title in every chunk. Generation neither fixes nor worsens that — it inherits whichever chunks the inflation surfaced. The answer itself is a fair synthesis of workload decomposition, per-workload autoscaling, and tail-latency observability.

queries.query: Who confirms that a delivery actually happened, and what does that confirmation trigger?
queries.comment: Partially relevant. Top-1 is the right section and does cover delivery confirmation triggering settlement, though it opens mid-sentence on the telematics signal rather than on proof of delivery. Top-2 drifts to CQRS Operational Realities on the strength of the word 'event'. The POD-to-settlement link is retrievable but not cleanly isolated in one chunk.
queries.hw3_comment: The flagship filter win. Baseline rank 2 was a CQRS chunk that drifted in on the word 'event'; the concept-guide filter (inferred from 'delivery'/'confirmation') evicts it, and the improved top-3 is all-primer — including The Load Lifecycle chunk that BM25 surfaces at lexical rank 1. Top-3 precision goes from 2/3 to 3/3. Crucially, hybrid-only made this query WORSE (the CQRS chunk reached top-1), so the gain here belongs to filtering and to filtering constraining hybrid — the clearest single demonstration of why the combined pipeline needs both parts.
queries.hw4_comment: The clearest demonstration in the set that answer generation is not just retrieval with prose on top. HW2's verdict on this query was that "the POD-to-settlement link is retrievable but not cleanly isolated in one chunk" — no single chunk carried the whole answer. The model assembled it from three, and produced the two-sentence answer HW2 said the corpus could not hand over directly: the consignee confirms via POD, and that confirmation triggers invoicing and settlement. All three chunks cited.

queries.query: What is the best way to fine-tune a large language model on a custom dataset?
queries.comment: Not relevant — correctly so, and this is the most useful query in the set. Nothing in a logistics corpus answers a question about fine-tuning language models, and the top score drops to 0.266, well clear of the 0.413 in-corpus floor. But the system still returns three confidently formatted results: a pure retrieval layer has no way to say 'I don't know'. A score floor near 0.35 would be needed before this feeds an LLM.
queries.hw3_comment: Correctly unfiltered — no inference rule matches, which is the designed behaviour: a filter would have funnelled an unanswerable question into one document and made the results look more authoritative than they are. Hybrid reshuffled which irrelevant chunks appear (BM25 latches onto 'model'-adjacent migration vocabulary), but the semantic ceiling is unchanged at 0.266, still well below the 0.413 in-corpus floor. The HW2 conclusion stands: only a score floor, out of scope here as in HW2, would let the system decline to answer.
queries.hw4_comment: Correct refusal, and the single most valuable result in the set. Top semantic is 0.266, below the 0.35 floor, so the context was passed empty and the model returned the refusal sentence with no citation and no source. This closes the thread HW2 opened and HW3 deferred: HW2 recorded that "a pure retrieval layer has no way to say 'I don't know'" and that a floor near 0.35 would be needed before this fed an LLM. It now does, and it works. The counterfactual is measured rather than asserted — case-1 in outputs/prompt_improvements.md runs this same question through the naive v1 prompt and gets a confident eight-step tutorial on LoRA and Hugging Face, none of it from the corpus.
